summary: A framework discussing how existing protocols and mechanisms could support Emergency Telecommunications Services within a single administrative domain. It comments on their potential use and current deployment but does not present specific solutions. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A plan for how a network could let emergency calls and messages go first, listing tools that might help without picking one.

questions: how can networks prioritize emergency traffic
what is ets emergency telecommunications service
what is a single administrative domain
subtitle: A survey of existing protocols that could help give emergency traffic better service inside one network.

tldr.problem: Operators who want to give Emergency Telecommunications Services (ETS) traffic better treatment inside their own network need to know which existing tools might help.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC limits itself to a single administrative domain and walks through candidates such as MPLS, RSVP, COPS policy control, link-layer priorities, multicast, service discovery and Diffserv, with comments on their use and deployment.
tldr.outcome: It names no specific solution. It leaves the choice to the reader, including the option of simply over-provisioning links.

today: RFC 4958 is an Informational RFC and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is a framework discussion and presents no specific solution.

sections.title: Scope and Objective
sections.content:
This framework looks at protocols that could support Emergency Telecommunications Services (ETS) within a single administrative domain, defined in the companion RFC 4375 as a collection of resources under the control of a single administrative authority. A related framework, RFC 4190, focused on IP telephony, whose flows can span many domains.

The objective is a target measure of service for flows labeled for ETS. That could be better than best effort, the best available service, or a specific percentage of resource set aside for ETS. The RFC stresses that discussing a protocol does not mean it exists in any given domain.

It considers two scenarios: a user in their home network, and a user visiting a foreign network. The second may be handled by DHCP or a static address set for visitors, or by Mobile IP.
sections.eli5: The goal is to give emergency messages a better lane inside one network, using tools that may or may not already be there.

sections.title: Why a Single Domain Is Easier
sections.content:
Each domain is an authority zone under separate management, and there is no scalable way to transfer authority between zones. Zones are often run by competitors. Different domains may apply different policies, and a transit domain has no practical way to authenticate every packet that carries an importance label.

The RFC argues that all current inter-domain QoS mechanisms at the network level create easily exploited Denial of Service attack vectors. A single domain, by contrast, can use access control lists in every edge device so that only authorized users emit non-default QoS labels, and can enforce its policies without trusting a third party.
sections.eli5: Inside your own house you can make the rules and check who follows them. Across many houses owned by different people, that is much harder.

sections.title: Over-Provisioning or QoS
sections.content:
The IEPREP working group debated whether it is always better to over-provision links so spikes still see no loss from congestion. Advocates point to cost effectiveness compared with the complexity and security issues of QoS mechanisms. Proponents of QoS reply that cheap bandwidth is not available everywhere and that some domains mix high-capacity fiber with lower-capacity wireless links.

The RFC advocates neither side. It does recommend that operators do a cost analysis of over-provisioning against QoS, and says that if they rely on over-provisioning, much of the rest of the document has little bearing, except for labeling used to talk to other architectures such as SIP-to-SS7/ISUP gateways.
sections.eli5: You can build a very wide road so nobody gets stuck, or you can add a special lane. The note says to work out which costs less for you.

sections.title: Signaling, Policy and Diffserv Candidates
sections.content:
MPLS builds Labeled Switched Paths, and RFC 3270 uses its 3-bit EXP field to convey a Per Hop Behavior. The RFC warns that MPLS is only one approach to traffic engineering and its complexity may suit only large domains.

RSVP (RFC 2205) reserves resources along a path. It has not been widely deployed across domains, and its limited use is mostly inside a domain alongside MPLS signaling. Reservations can help an emergency flow get forwarded, but major vendor routers mostly classify only on network and transport layer fields, so application layer labels are likely ignored.

Policy control uses COPS (RFC 2748), where Policy Enforcement Points query Policy Decision Points; RFC 2749 covers its use with RSVP. The text notes that COPS was discussed at the 60th IETF in 2004 as a candidate to be declared historic because of lack of use.

Diffserv (RFC 2474) has been deployed within domains. The RFC argues its Assured Forwarding and Expedited Forwarding behaviors may exceed what ETS needs, and that simpler queuing such as class-based weighted fair queuing may suffice.
sections.eli5: These are different kinds of lane markings and traffic cops. Some are heavy machinery, and a simpler lane may be enough.

sections.title: Link Layers, Multicast and Discovery
sections.content:
At layer 2, the IEEE 802.1 VLAN tag carries a 3-bit Prioritization field with 8 levels, the highest being 7. Because of the scarcity of bits, ETS traffic should expect to share a priority level with other important traffic, with no exclusive value reserved for it. 802.11e adds 8 traffic categories to wireless LANs but offers no guarantee of service. For cable networks, DOCSIS 1.1 added support beyond best effort, though it leaves classification, policing and scheduling to vendors.

Multicast can efficiently reach many receivers, which fits the push-to-talk style of land mobile radio used by first responders. Integrating LMR talk groups with IP multicast is described as an open issue. The RFC also warns that multicast can enable denial of service, which source-specific multicast with access lists reduces.

To find ETS-aware servers, the RFC mentions the Service Location Protocol (RFC 2608), anycast (RFC 1546) and the Dynamic Delegation Discovery System (RFC 3401).
sections.eli5: Even the wires and Wi-Fi underneath have small priority labels, but only a few, so emergency traffic must share its label with other important traffic.

sections.title: Security Considerations and Summary
sections.content:
Services that offer better service to a set of users are prime targets for attack or misuse. Administrators who add protocols for ETS are strongly encouraged to adopt new policies for the added risk, independent of any mechanism that restricts access to the domain. Authorization is called an open issue: an access list of permitted multicast senders may be acceptable in one domain, while other services need detailed credentials and multiple levels of access.

The summary says the protocols were chosen because all or most of them can be operated within one domain. Protocols still under development in the NSIS working group are therefore not covered. By listing many options the RFC avoids picking a winner and leaves the choice to the reader.
sections.eli5: A special lane tempts cheaters, so you need rules for who may use it. The note lists options and lets you choose.

items.title: MPLS
items.text: Labeled paths; 3-bit EXP field carries the Per Hop Behavior.

items.title: RSVP
items.text: Reserves resources, mostly used inside a domain.

items.title: Policy (COPS)
items.text: Policy servers decide whether to accept reservations.

items.title: Discovery
items.text: SLP, anycast and DDDS to find ETS servers.

items.title: Diffserv
items.text: AF and EF behaviors, possibly more than ETS needs.
